analysis.one_liner: Removes the $75 million liability cap on offshore oil spills and funds home energy retrofits, electric vehicles, and Gulf restoration.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Majority Leader weeks after the BP spill, the bill sat on the Senate calendar and never came to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in response to the April 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster, the bill would make offshore oil companies pay unlimited cleanup and damage costs instead of being capped at $75 million above removal costs. It also would break up the Interior Department office that both leased drilling and regulated it, raise fines for safety violations, require disclosure of fracking chemicals, and create rebate and loan programs for home energy retrofits, electric vehicles, and natural gas trucks. The bill was introduced on July 28, 2010, read twice, placed on the Senate calendar, and never taken up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents and taxpayers, who would no longer be on the hook when an offshore spill exceeds an oil company's insurance; Gulf communities and fishing businesses, who would get faster claims processing, better spill response, and long-term Gulf restoration; workers and homeowners, who could qualify for Home Star retrofit rebates and financing; and workers on rigs, who would get new training standards.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the statutory cap that limited an offshore facility operator's liability for damages to $75 million beyond removal costs, so the responsible company—not taxpayers—pays for a catastrophic spill.

Requires Interior's offshore regulators to be separated from its leasing and revenue offices so the agency collecting drilling money is not the same one policing safety, and allows the NTSB to independently investigate offshore accidents.
Speeds the claims process so spill victims can be paid within 30 days rather than 90, and lets the Coast Guard draw on the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund during a spill of national significance.

Creates Home Star rebate and loan programs for home energy upgrades and a national plug-in electric vehicle deployment program, plus a natural gas vehicle and infrastructure program funded by an increased per-barrel oil tax.

Requires companies drilling in water deeper than 500 feet to submit deepwater operations plans using best available blowout-prevention technology, and mandates certified training for offshore workers.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, through unlimited spill liability, higher civil penalties, new inspection fees, and costlier safety equipment; all oil producers and ultimately consumers through a 45-cents-per-barrel increase in the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund financing rate; and federal taxpayers, who fund the retrofit, electric-vehicle, and research programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil companies and oil consumers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund financing rate to 45 cents a barrel, a cost that refiners could pass to consumers at the pump.

Unlimited liability and stricter permitting and inspection requirements would raise offshore drilling costs, which oil companies argue could slow Gulf production and affect the jobs and small businesses tied to it—the bill itself directs DOE to study the drilling moratorium's effect on employment.
Retroactive liability applies to claims arising from events before enactment, which critics said changed legal rules after the fact and raised costs for companies that had planned around the old cap.
The Home Star and electric-vehicle programs are new federal spending and loan guarantees whose benefits flow through private contractors and manufacturers, adding administrative cost to every rebate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core liability change closes a real gap: under the 1990 law a company causing a catastrophic spill could shed most damages above a small cap, leaving taxpayers and coastal residents to absorb the rest. The cost is higher drilling expenses and a modestly higher per-barrel tax that may reach gas prices, plus new federal spending on retrofits and vehicles whose value depends on program execution. On balance the benefits to taxpayers and coastal communities outweigh those costs, though the bill was a large, sprawling package assembled quickly that never received committee scrutiny.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Majority Leader introduced it, it was placed on the Senate calendar, and it never came to the floor for debate or a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Harry Reid introduced the bill on July 28, 2010, roughly three months after the Deepwater Horizon explosion, as the Senate's comprehensive response to the spill.
The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 29, 2010, but no committee acted on it and no further floor action ever occurred.
No senator cosponsored the bill, including among Democrats.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and all legislation not enacted died with it, including this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil producers kept the $75 million liability cap and avoided the stricter safety rules, higher penalties, and inspection fees, and no new federal retrofit or electric-vehicle programs were created. Taxpayers and coastal communities gained nothing.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, then moved it onto the Senate calendar as the chamber's response to the BP spill.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed Congress after the Deepwater Horizon disaster to pass legislation raising oil company liability and overhauling offshore drilling oversight.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Led Senate Republicans in opposing the spill-response bill, arguing the liability change and drilling restrictions would cost jobs, and the bill never advanced to the floor.

against.name: Offshore drilling industry
against.role: Oil and gas producers and trade associations
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against unlimited liability and the new offshore safety and fee requirements during the post-spill debate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had zero cosponsors of either party, and no Republican supported it; as the chamber's Democratic leadership vehicle it never reached a recorded vote, so no roll-call numbers exist.

industries.note: The bill strips the $75 million cap on spill damages, raises civil penalties, adds inspection fees, requires deepwater operations plans and safety-case documentation, and can disqualify companies that failed to pay spill obligations from new leases. Because a major spill's costs otherwise fall on taxpayers and coastal communities, the industry's savings here come at the public's expense.
The Home Star rebate and loan programs would pay homeowners to hire certified contractors for energy upgrades, creating work in construction trades.
Deployment grants, loan guarantees for battery purchases, federal fleet purchases, and research prizes would build demand for domestic EV and battery production.

industries.industry: Natural gas vehicle and fueling sector
industries.note: A new DOE program offers rebates, infrastructure grants, and manufacturing loans to build out natural gas trucks and fueling stations.
The bill requires more frequent and comprehensive safety inspections and revises vessel liability limits, raising compliance costs for shippers who move oil by sea.

Faster claims processing, required advance planning for closing and reopening fishing grounds, and Gulf restoration and monitoring programs would protect the resource base these businesses depend on after a spill.
